rubric.why: Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction.
rubric.description: States that work involves force and displacement in the direction of the force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying force and displacement as necessary for work.

rubric.why: Energy is defined as the capacity to do work.
rubric.description: Defines energy as the capacity to do work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of energy.

modelAnswer: Work is done when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force.
Energy is the capacity to do work.
Both work and energy are measured in joules (J).

items.followUp: What are the fixed points used to calibrate a Celsius thermometer?

rubric.why: The lower fixed point is the temperature of melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the lower fixed point as 0°C, the melting point of ice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the lower fixed point correctly.

rubric.why: The upper fixed point is the temperature of steam above boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the upper fixed point as 100°C, the boiling point of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the upper fixed point correctly.

modelAnswer: The lower fixed point of a thermometer is the temperature of melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure; it is 0°C on the Celsius scale.
The upper fixed point is the temperature of steam above boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure; it is 100°C on the Celsius scale.

rubric.why: The Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion relation is required.
rubric.description: Writes the correct conversion formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formula.

rubric.why: Substitution of 50°C gives 122°F.
rubric.description: Substitutes the temperature and gives the correct Fahrenheit result with unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 122°F.

modelAnswer: Given: C = 50°C
Formula: F = (9/5)C + 32
Answer: F = 122°F

items.followUp: State the conditions for an object to float on or sink in water.

rubric.why: An object with lower density than water floats; its weight is balanced by the upthrust when floating.
rubric.description: States the condition for floating.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the object's density is less than water's, or that upthrust balances its weight.

rubric.why: An object with greater density than water sinks; its weight exceeds the upthrust.
rubric.description: States the condition for sinking.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the object's density is greater than water's, or that its weight exceeds the upthrust.

modelAnswer: An object floats on water when its density is less than the density of water; while floating, the upthrust balances its weight.
An object sinks in water when its density is greater than the density of water, so its weight is greater than the upthrust.

items.followUp: What are the charged particles in plasma, and how do they carry electric current?

rubric.why: Plasma is an ionized gas containing free electrons and positive ions.
rubric.description: Defines plasma as an ionized gas containing charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition and identification of its charged particles.

rubric.description: Relates plasma to electric current through movement of charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that moving charged particles carry current.

modelAnswer: Plasma is an ionized gas containing free electrons and positive ions.
It conducts electric current because its charged particles move and carry charge.

items.followUp: Using a speed-time graph, derive the expression S = Vᵢt + ½at².

rubric.why: Displacement is represented by the area under the speed-time graph.
rubric.description: Recognizes the area under the graph as displacement and divides it into rectangle and triangle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the graph-area interpretation.

rubric.why: The rectangular area under the graph is Vᵢt.
rubric.description: Finds the rectangular area as initial speed times time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the rectangular area.

rubric.why: The triangular area is ½(Vf − Vᵢ)t, and Vf − Vᵢ = at.
rubric.description: Finds the triangular area and uses the acceleration relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the triangular area with the correct velocity change.

rubric.why: Adding the two areas gives the required displacement equation.
rubric.description: Obtains the required expression for displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final expression.

modelAnswer: Displacement S equals the area under the speed-time graph.
The area consists of a rectangle and a triangle.
Rectangle area = Vᵢ × t = Vᵢt.
Triangle area = ½ × (Vf − Vᵢ) × t.
Since a = (Vf − Vᵢ)/t, then Vf − Vᵢ = at.
Therefore, S = Vᵢt + ½at².

items.followUp: Find the acceleration produced by a force of 120 N acting on a mass of 30 kg.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the given force and mass.
rubric.description: Lists the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying F = 100 N and m = 50 kg.

rubric.why: Newton's second law gives a = F/m.
rubric.description: Writes the applicable formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation.

rubric.why: Substitution gives the force divided by the mass.
rubric.description: Substitutes the given values with units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution.

rubric.why: The resulting acceleration is 2 m/s².
rubric.description: Gives the correct acceleration with unit.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for 2 m/s²; award 1 mark if the numerical result is correct but the unit is missing or incorrect.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 100 N, m = 50 kg
Formula: a = F/m
Substitution: a = 100 N / 50 kg
Answer: a = 2 m/s²

items.followUp: Define potential energy and derive its expression for an object at height h above Earth.

rubric.why: Potential energy is associated with an object's position or configuration.
rubric.description: Defines potential energy in terms of position or configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: The energy stored is equal to the work done in lifting the object against gravity.
rubric.description: Explains that lifting against gravity requires work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the work done against gravity.

rubric.why: Work is force multiplied by displacement; here F = mg and the vertical displacement is h.
rubric.description: Applies the work relation with gravitational force and height.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using F = mg and displacement h in the work calculation.

rubric.why: The work done is stored as gravitational potential energy, giving PE = mgh.
rubric.description: Derives the final expression for gravitational potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final expression.

modelAnswer: Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object because of its position or configuration.
To raise an object of mass m through height h, work is done against gravity.
Work done, W = force × displacement.
The force required to lift the object is its weight, F = mg, and the displacement is h.
Therefore, W = Fh = mgh.
This work is stored as gravitational potential energy, so PE = mgh.
